policy_title: Improve school funding, teacher pay, and infrastructure
stated: Advocate for an £8bn investment in schools, including £2bn for a teacher pay uplift, and invest £2.5bn a year to tackle the RAAC concrete scandal and ensure school buildings are safe and well-maintained. This includes investing £5bn in special needs (SEND) provision within mainstream schools to ensure accessible buildings, specially trained teachers, and proper support for SEND students, including transport.

source.quote: Elected Greens will: • Advocate for an increase in school funding, with an £8bn investment in schools that would include £2bn for a pay uplift for teachers. • Ensure that every school building is safe for children by investing £2.5bn a year to tackle the RAAC concrete scandal and provide the funding needed for schools to be well-maintained and fit for purpose. Green MPs will push for £5bn to be invested in special needs (SEND) provision within mainstream schools. This means that all schools will have fully accessible buildings and specially trained teachers, and local councils will have the funds to properly support SEND students at school and in getting to school.

consolidated_from: Increase school funding and teacher pay
Invest in special educational needs provision

bearing_set.reason: Direct investment in school funding, teacher pay, SEND provision, and building infrastructure materially affects school standards, attainment (especially for SEND pupils), and educational opportunity.
£2bn explicit teacher pay uplift directly improves wages and conditions for ~500,000 public-sector workers, a non-negligible effect on a specific workforce's real pay.

£5bn SEND provision specifically targets equal access and anti-discrimination protections for disabled pupils — accessible buildings, specialist staff, and transport are equal-treatment obligations, making this a concrete bearing on minority protections and equal treatment.

Combined commitment (£8bn schools + £2.5bn/year recurring RAAC + £5bn SEND) is materially large; absent a stated funding source, this represents a substantial addition to public expenditure with a plausible bearing on debt-path sustainability.

membership_note: Four fundamentals bear on this policy: it is primarily an O7 education measure, with an explicit O4 labour-market effect for teachers, a genuine O9 equal-treatment dimension for SEND pupils, and a non-trivial O12 fiscal footprint from the scale of unfunded/unspecified spending. O13 (long-run productivity) is plausible but too indirect at membership stage; O14 (inequality) routes through O7 and O9 rather than income/wealth gap directly.
